prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength brought atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from the Higgs case (B026) to optical lattice clocks with Katori and Ye. The scientific reasoning is unchanged: I still regard the Higgs observation as the most important result on this shortlist, and I still weigh discoveries of nature most heavily. What has changed is my assessment of whether the committee can stand behind a specific credit. The chair asked for a principle for choosing three names for B026 and for what each did in the 2012 observation. I cannot give that. My round-1 argument rested on founding proposers and leaders, my colleagues have shown that this is a proxy for organisational leadership and not for the act of discovery, and I said myself that the committee should turn elsewhere if no defensible three names exist. For B042 the situation is the opposite. The magic-wavelength proposal removes the trap light shift so that many neutral atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime, and this is an identifiable idea with an identifiable originator. Ye's group then showed that the architecture could deliver systematic uncertainties near 1e-18, and independent laboratories have reproduced that in several species and compared clocks across sites. Maturity is not in doubt, and I do not regard the pending redefinition of the second as part of the case. I will concede the point that moved me: this is not only a refinement of the comb and single-ion work honoured in 2005 and 2012, because the many-atom, light-shift-cancelled lattice is a different principle with a different error budget. I still think a prize for a better measurement is a smaller statement than one for the origin of mass, but a prize that can be written precisely and defended name by name is the better prize.
statement.case_against: The credit boundary is not closed. Takamoto and Ido demonstrated the strontium lattice clock, Lemonde's group made comparable contributions, and a two-name prize leaves all of them out; the citation must therefore be written around the lattice concept and its demonstrated performance and claim no more. Ye's name is also tied to comb and cavity-stabilised-laser work already adjacent to the 2005 prize and to the thorium nuclear clock, which I would keep out of the citation. There is a real overlap question with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and a reader may still call this incremental. Finally, I have not verified the first-demonstration priorities from primary sources, and I am aware that my move toward the option with the strongest first-round support could be accepted too easily; I have tried to base it on the attribution argument and not on the count.

responses.point: Lindroth warns that agreement among members with an atomic-physics vantage is not evidence of merit, and that the test is whether colleagues outside AMO find the conceptual step substantial. She also names the control of blackbody, higher-order light shift and hyperpolarisability effects as what made the lattice a real clock.
responses.response: I am one of the colleagues outside AMO, and I take the test seriously. My answer is that the conceptual step is substantial: cancelling the trap light shift for the clock transition is a simple idea that removes the obstacle which kept neutral atoms from being used, and the hundredfold gain in accuracy followed from it. Her point about blackbody and higher-order shifts persuades me that the credit for Ye is for the demonstrated 1e-18 realisation and not just for the comb and laser infrastructure around it. I still hold that this does not answer a question comparable to the origin of mass, so I move to B042 on attribution and maturity, not because the physics outranks the Higgs result.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the many-atom, light-shift-cancelled lattice is a new principle and not a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and that the citation should rest on what has been demonstrated, not on the pending redefinition of the second. He also asks which analysis or detector contributions would justify the three Higgs names.
responses.response: His challenge on B026 is fair and I have no concrete answer, which is the main reason I have moved. I also accept his distinction between the comb as a ruler, control of single quantum systems and the lattice architecture, and I agree with him that the citation should not lean on the redefinition. Where I would go further than he does is on Ye: I would write the citation so that his credit is clearly for the lattice clock and its record comparisons, as he proposes, and I would not let the nuclear clock appear in the text.

responses.point: Pearce prefers IceCube with Halzen and Spiering as a discovery of nature through a kilometre-scale detector, with a two-name credit that avoids the leadership-proxy problem, and he lists his Fermi-LAT link to the TXS 0506+056 follow-up as a disclosed connection.
responses.response: I still regard B029 as a strong alternative and would support Halzen and Spiering, and I agree that it avoids the leadership problem that sank my own first choice. My reservation is that the diffuse flux is secure but the population origin and the source identification are still developing, so I would put it behind B042 for now. On his disclosed Fermi-LAT link, I think the committee should treat it as a collaboration-level connection and note it; I would not ask him to recuse unless B029 becomes the leading ballot, in which case the committee should decide that openly.

responses.point: Johansson disagrees with the leadership-as-proxy attribution for the Higgs, asks what concretely each of Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee contributed to the 2012 observation, and wants the clock citation framed around the lattice architecture and its 1e-18 performance.
responses.response: I agree with him on both points. I cannot say what each of the three contributed to the observation itself, and rewarding organisational leadership as a stand-in for discovery is exactly what I should not defend. I accept his wording for the clock citation, framed around the lattice architecture and its performance, and I would not add the thorium clock. I also respect his decision to step back from circuit QED, and I add only that Takamoto, Ido and Lemonde can be left outside a two-name prize defensibly only if the citation is narrow, so the wording must carry the weight.

uncertainties: Whether Takamoto, Ido or Lemonde have a first-demonstration claim strong enough that a two-name prize is contestable, which I cannot settle from the supplied material.

Whether the committee will see the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether my own acceptance of this is influenced by the concentration of support among AMO colleagues.
Whether the Higgs result will ever get a defensible three-name credit; I have set B026 aside for now on attribution, not on merit, and each year of delay makes the question harder.
For IceCube, how to word a citation fair to Baikal, DUMAND, AMANDA and ANTARES while naming only Halzen and Spiering, and whether source identification will mature further.
I am relying on my own knowledge of the history and have not verified individual roles in any of these collaborations or laboratories.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. I worked at CERN for two years in the early 1990s, before ATLAS and CMS were built, with no documented tie to Della Negra, Jenni or Virdee; I flag it for transparency since B026 is now only an alternative. My profile shows no connection to Katori or Ye, or to Halzen or Spiering. Nothing in the round-1 exchange changes this disclosure.
